newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese frowns won't stop dollar rising -- dealers.
newsitem.headline: Japanese frowns won't stop dollar rising -- dealers.

text.p: Buoyed by a battered yen, the dollar is expected to head higher in the New Year as markets take little notice of monetary authorities' apparent concern at its excessive rise, analysts and dealers said.

"We may see the dollar at 117 yen in the New Year. With both (Japanese) stocks and bonds in such a dismal state, there's no incentive to buy the yen," said Nobumitsu Watanabe, manager of foreign exchange trade at Yasuda Trust & Banking Co.
The dollar pierced the key 115 yen barrier on Thursday for the first time in over 44 months, rising to 115.12 yen on the back of a plunge in Tokyo shares.
It then ebbed, standing at about 114.70 yen in late trade.

In the stock market, the benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares briefly dipped to 18,819.92, the first time it had been below the key 19,000 level since December 6, 1995. It clawed back later to end down 257.83 points at 19,291.58.

Weakness in share prices has strengthened the view that Japan will be forced to keep its interest rates at record lows, leaving the yen less attractive than currencies with higher yields such as the dollar.
Apart from frail stocks, a recent sell-off of yen bonds has aroused concerns of a "triple weakness", in which the yen is sold as capital flows out of Japanese stocks and bonds.
The benchmark March Japanese government bond futures ended Thursday trade sharply lower, down 0.35 at 124.95.
Although dealers said Japanese exporters' sales braked any further rise in the dollar on Thursday, many exporters seem to share dealers' expectations of a stronger dollar.

"We plan to sell (the dollar) whenever it sets a new high, but we're in no rush to sell for our future requirements amid this bullish sentiment," said Akira Shimura, manager of foreign exchange at electronics giant Toshiba Corp.
In contrast with the bullish outlook of many in the market, monetary authorities appear to be concerned at the possibility of an excessive rise in the dollar.
Analysts said authorities were worried about the yen weakening beyond 115 yen, as such a movement would be out of line with economic fundamentals and would harm Japan's economy.

"Should the dollar rise again above 115 yen and show signs of a further appreciation, comments to check such rises will likely emerge from the authorities," said Takao Sakoh, first vice president with Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) in Tokyo.

Officials at both the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and the Ministry of Finance (MOF) were careful not to touch on specific levels on Thursday, but some of their comments aroused speculation that they were dissatisfied with the rise above 115 yen.
A senior MOF official told Reuters: "Japanese monetary authorities do not welcome wild fluctuations in foreign exchange rates," adding that they were keeping close watch on currency movements.
Separately, a senior BOJ official also said the central bank was carefully monitoring developments in the market.
The comments spurred selling of dollars bought during the rise above 115 yen, but did not persuade most dealers to alter their bullish outlook.
"The comments may temporarily put a lid on the dollar's rise but may not be able to reverse the trend its further rise on a longer-term basis," said a dealer at a long-term credit bank in Tokyo.

But Sakoh at UBS said market participants should take more note of the comments. "They're moderate, but are very important messages. It's the second round," he said, referring to comments by a key MOF official in November interpreted as a sign of authorities' discontent with the dollar's rise.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, said then that the market's view on Japan's economy was too pessimistic and he believed it was stronger than the market thought.
The comment, coming soon after the dollar hit 114.92 yen, the year's high at the time, invited a flurry of dollar sales.
